summary:
Picture an astronaut on the way to Mars. A message home takes minutes to
arrive, and the nearest doctor is millions of miles away. Something feels off,
maybe poor sleep, a low mood, a racing heartbeat, and the only person who can
make sense of it is the astronaut. That is why we chose this challenge. As
missions go deeper into space, crews will have to understand their own health,
and NASA’s research on the risks exists but is spread across too many pages to
use in the moment.
Cosmos Health brings it together. Each day, the astronaut enters a quick check-
in covering sleep, mood, heart rate, blood pressure, exercise and more, along
with their lifestyle and surroundings. The app learns what is normal for that
person and, using NASA’s Human Research Program, estimates which of the five
spaceflight hazards is most likely behind any change. Each hazard gets a
probability, and the app suggests lifestyle adjustments that fit the leading one,
every suggestion linked to its NASA source.
We chose this over a simple tracker because numbers alone don’t answer the
question that matters: why is this happening, and what can I do about it?
Waiting for advice from Earth doesn’t work when every reply is delayed. And
because every answer traces back to NASA, the crew can check the reasoning
instead of just trusting it.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Cosmos Health is a self-check web app for astronauts. The astronaut picks a

mission environment (space station, deep-space craft, rover or surface base) and

enters daily indicators such as sleep, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and

exercise. The app links these inputs to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards: radiation,

isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity, and closed

environment. Each hazard gets a score from 0 to 100, and the highest one is

shown as the top match. The app also has a clickable body map, which links body

regions to cited NASA risks, and a symptom log. It gives short, sourced

explanations and recommendations suited to the leading hazard and the

environment.

How does it work?

Every slider is compared with its baseline value, and the difference is

normalized to a 0 to 100 scale. Each indicator is mapped to the hazards that

NASA’s risk records connect to the body system it belongs to. A hazard’s score is

the average deviation of its linked inputs. Sliders and body regions shift from

green to red as inputs move away from the baseline. The environment changes

the context shown (which indicators matter most, how each hazard applies

there) but not the calculation. Every factual statement comes from a data file

that links it to NASA or Canadian Space Agency sources, and the project’s own

wording is kept separate and labeled.

What benefits does it have?

It gathers scattered NASA research and daily health signals in one place.

It supports self-reliance when real-time medical help is far away.

It explains why a pattern may matter, not just what the numbers are.

Every claim can be traced to its source.

It is transparent about its limits: scores are a simulated index, not

probabilities, and no clinical thresholds are invented.

What do you hope to achieve?

We hope to show how a simple, sourced self-check could help deep-space crews

make sense of their own health. Next, we would calibrate the scoring with NASA

researchers and flight surgeons, connect real mission sensors, and refine the

environment-specific recommendations. The aim is to grow from an educational

prototype into a tool validated for use on real missions.

What tools, languages and software did you use?

Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

3D visuals: Three.js (r128), loaded from a CDN.

Typography: Google Fonts (Dela Gothic One and Barlow Semi Condensed).

Data: one structured JSON file holding NASA/CSA-sourced facts, indicator

settings, environment content and the scoring rules.

Storage: browser-only, with nothing sent to a server.

Testing: Python unittest with Playwright browser checks.

AI assistance: Claude for coding and bug fixing, and Manus for web scraping

and data cleaning.

Hardware simulation: none. The sliders simulate inputs, and no real sensors

or live mission data are connected.
